initial_requirements: Scientists and software engineers need a Model Manager that automates the setup and operation of computational model jobs across one or more clusters. Users should be able to configure, schedule, submit, monitor, stop, restart, and resume operational, research, post-processing, or existing scripted jobs. The system should manage nodes and choose execution resources while still allowing experienced users to request a particular cluster when necessary.

turns.interviewer_utterance:
Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about the Model Manager project so we can understand the needs, workflows, and priorities clearly.

Before we begin, are you aligned with this interview scope, or do you expect something different?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, that scope sounds right to me. I’m aligned with discussing how Model Manager should set up, submit, monitor, and control jobs across clusters, along with how it should handle resource selection and user overrides. If there’s anything outside that, I’ll say so.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Thank you. To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?
turns.interviewee_utterance: I’m here as a stakeholder representing the people who will use and operate Model Manager, mainly the scientists and software engineers who run computational jobs. My connection is that I understand the day-to-day workflow problems this system needs to solve, especially around scheduling, cluster usage, and job control.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Thanks. Could you describe the current process or system you use today for setting up, submitting, monitoring, and controlling these computational jobs across clusters?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Today it’s mostly a mix of manual scripts, cluster-specific submission commands, and a few ad hoc conventions that different teams have evolved over time. People usually prepare the job configuration themselves, choose a cluster based on experience or availability, submit it directly, and then monitor it through cluster tools or logs. Stopping, restarting, or resuming jobs can be pretty inconsistent and often depends on the job type and what the script supports.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Ok, what current processes do you want to change or improve, or what features do you hope to get from Model Manager?
turns.interviewee_utterance: We want to remove as much manual setup and cluster-specific handling as possible so users can use one consistent way to manage jobs. A big improvement would be letting the system choose the best execution resources automatically, while still allowing power users to pick a specific cluster when they really need to. We also want better control over job lifecycle actions like stopping, restarting, and resuming without having to rely on custom scripts every time.

turns.interviewer_utterance:
So far, I understand the main features as:
- one consistent way to configure and manage jobs
- automated resource / cluster selection
- optional user override to request a specific cluster
- better job lifecycle control: submit, monitor, stop, restart, resume

Are there any other features you would like to see in Model Manager?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Those are the main ones, yes. One other thing that would matter is supporting different job types cleanly, like operational, research, post-processing, and already scripted jobs, since they don’t all behave the same way. Beyond that, I’d also want good visibility into job status and failures so users can tell what happened without digging through cluster logs.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Based on your description, do you think support for different job types should include different setup templates or workflows for each type?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, that would make sense. Some job types probably need different setup defaults or slightly different submission steps, especially if a scripted job already has its own structure. I’d expect the system to handle those differences without making users relearn the whole process each time.

turns.interviewer_utterance:
Understood. So the main features/functions we have identified are:
- a consistent job management workflow
- automated execution resource / cluster selection
- user override to request a specific cluster
- job lifecycle control: submit, monitor, stop, restart, resume
- support for multiple job types
- different setup defaults and submission steps by job type
- clear job status and failure visibility

Are there any other features you would like to see in this project, or should we treat this list as complete?
turns.interviewee_utterance: I think that covers the core needs pretty well. If anything else comes up, it would probably be more of a nice-to-have than a must-have, so for now I’d treat this list as basically complete.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Thanks. Of the features we’ve identified, which are the highest priority?
turns.interviewee_utterance: The highest priority is getting the core job workflow working end to end: configure, submit, monitor, and control jobs in one place. Right after that, automated cluster selection is very important because that’s where a lot of the manual effort and confusion is today. Support for different job types is also important, but I’d rank it slightly behind those two.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Please elaborate on what you want this core job workflow to accomplish.
turns.interviewee_utterance: It should let a user define a job once, have the system prepare it correctly for the target environment, and then submit it without needing separate cluster-specific steps. After submission, the user should be able to see the status clearly and take actions like stop, restart, or resume from the same place. Ideally it also reduces the need to know the underlying cluster details unless the user explicitly wants to override them.

turns.interviewer_utterance: It seems like you need a single end-to-end job workflow with environment preparation, submission, status visibility, and lifecycle actions. Can you describe more about what “prepare it correctly for the target environment” should do?
turns.interviewee_utterance: That would mainly mean applying the right configuration for the cluster and job type, like resource settings, queue or scheduler parameters, and any environment-specific variables or paths. It should also handle any required setup differences between operational, research, post-processing, or scripted jobs so users don’t have to do that manually. If there are cluster-specific constraints, the system should account for them automatically unless the user has chosen a specific cluster.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Understood. Do you have a current system in place for this preparation step, or is it entirely manual today?
turns.interviewee_utterance: It’s mostly manual today, with users and engineers doing a lot of the environment-specific setup themselves. There may be some scripts or conventions already in use, but I wouldn’t call it a single managed system yet.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What should happen if the system cannot automatically determine the best cluster or execution resources for a job?
turns.interviewee_utterance: If it can’t determine the best choice confidently, it should not guess in a risky way. I’d expect it to either fall back to a safe default or ask the user to choose a cluster explicitly, depending on what information is missing. It should also make it clear why it couldn’t decide so the user can correct the job settings.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Thank you. Could you describe what kinds of information or indicators Model Manager should use to choose the best cluster or execution resources?
turns.interviewee_utterance: It should use the job’s resource needs, like CPU, memory, runtime expectations, and maybe any GPU or special node requirements if those apply. It should also consider cluster availability, current load, and whether the job type has known preferences or restrictions for certain environments. If the user has specified a cluster or other constraints, those should override the automatic choice.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What level of control should users have when they override the automatic cluster selection?
turns.interviewee_utterance: They should be able to explicitly choose the cluster, and probably also set the main execution parameters that matter for placement, like the queue or partition if that’s exposed. I wouldn’t want them to have to micromanage every internal detail, but experienced users should be able to bypass the recommendation when they know a particular cluster is required. Ideally the system still validates the choice and warns them if it looks incompatible.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you describe more about how you want job status and failures to be shown to users?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Users should be able to see a simple live status like queued, running, stopped, failed, or completed, plus basic progress or timing information if it’s available. If a job fails, the system should surface the reason in plain language and include enough detail for a scientist or engineer to understand whether it was a setup issue, a resource issue, or a runtime error. I’d also want a clear link back to logs or diagnostics so they can act on it without digging through cluster tools.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Who else do you think has valuable insights into the project, and whose needs need to be considered, and why?
turns.interviewee_utterance: The main people are the scientists who run the models, because they care about ease of use and getting jobs set up correctly, and the software engineers or platform team, because they need the system to fit the cluster environment and be maintainable. I’d also include operations or support folks, since they usually deal with failures, resource issues, and user questions. If there’s a scheduler or HPC admin group, their constraints matter too because they can affect what the system is actually allowed to do.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What would make you consider the deployment of Model Manager successful?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Success would mean people can submit and manage jobs with much less manual effort and fewer mistakes than today. I’d also want to see that it works reliably across the target clusters, with clear status visibility and controls for stopping, restarting, and resuming jobs when needed. If users trust the cluster selection enough that they only override it in special cases, that would be a strong sign it’s working well.

turns.interviewer_utterance:
To summarize, we discussed:
- a single end-to-end workflow to configure, prepare, submit, monitor, and control jobs
- automated cluster/resource selection using job needs, availability, and job-type preferences
- user override for explicit cluster choice and some placement parameters
- support for operational, research, post-processing, and scripted jobs with different defaults/steps
- clear status, failure reasons, and links to logs/diagnostics
- success measured by reduced manual effort, fewer mistakes, reliable multi-cluster operation, and user trust in recommendations

Is there anything else you would like to add?
turns.interviewee_utterance: One thing I’d add is auditability, so we can tell who submitted or changed a job and what settings were used. I’d also want the system to handle resubmission or restart cleanly after a failure, because that’s a common operational need. Otherwise, that summary sounds very close to what we need.
